periods.title: Exploring Alhambra
periods.text: Begin your day at Alhambra early to beat the crowds and catch the best light. The main site is most atmospheric in the morning when the air is cool and the landscape catches the first golden rays. Take time to explore the main highlights and capture photographs in the soft morning light. This is the most rewarding time to visit.
periods.tip: Arrive as early as possible. The first hour after opening has the fewest visitors and the best photography conditions.

periods.title: Deeper Exploration
periods.text: Spend the afternoon exploring further afield. Explore the surrounding areas, museums, or lesser-known sections that most visitors miss. Grab lunch at a local eatery for authentic flavours and budget-friendly prices.
periods.tip: Midday sun can be intense, so bring sunscreen, a hat, and plenty of water. Rest during the hottest hours if needed.

periods.title: Golden Hour & Farewell
periods.text: End the day watching the golden hour transform the landscape. The evening light at Alhambra is spectacular and worth waiting for. Find a local restaurant for dinner of European cuisine with local wine.
periods.tip: Sunset times vary by season, so check ahead and position yourself 30 minutes early for the best spot.

periods.title: Nasrid Palaces at Opening
periods.text: Enter the Nasrid Palaces the moment they open. Your timed ticket (€14 combined entry) dictates your slot, so be at the gate 15 minutes early. Walk through the Mexuar council chamber, the ornate Comares Hall with its 16-metre cedar ceiling, and the legendary Court of the Lions, whose 124 marble columns are among the finest examples of Moorish art anywhere in the world.
periods.tip: Book Nasrid Palace tickets on the official Alhambra website weeks ahead, as same-day availability is virtually impossible in peak season.

periods.title: Alcazaba Fortress & Panoramic Views
periods.text: Cross to the Alcazaba, the oldest part of the complex, dating to the 9th century. Climb the Torre de la Vela for sweeping views over Granada's Albaicín quarter and the Sierra Nevada beyond. The watchtower's bell once rang to control irrigation across the Vega plain. Grab lunch at the Parador de Granada inside the complex, pricey but the setting in a converted convent is extraordinary.
periods.tip: The Alcazaba is included in the combined Alhambra ticket. Visit after the Nasrid Palaces to avoid the midday rush at the fortress.

periods.title: Albaicín at Sunset from Mirador San Nicolás
periods.text: Descend into Granada's Moorish quarter, the Albaicín, a UNESCO World Heritage neighbourhood of whitewashed houses and cobblestone lanes. Make your way to Mirador de San Nicolás by 7pm for a view of the Alhambra palace bathed in golden light against the snow-dusted Sierra Nevada, widely considered one of Spain's greatest views. Dine nearby on tapas; Granada still offers free tapas with every drink.
periods.tip: The Albaicín is hilly, so wear comfortable shoes. Pickpockets target the mirador; keep bags in front and phones in your pocket.

periods.title: Generalife Palace & Terraced Gardens
periods.text: Return to the Alhambra complex to explore the Generalife, the Nasrid sultans' summer estate. The Acequia garden, a long reflecting pool flanked by cypress and rose hedges with water jets, is one of the oldest surviving Islamic gardens in the world. The upper terraces offer quieter views over the palace complex that most day visitors never reach. Allow 90 minutes to do it justice.
periods.tip: The Generalife is included in the combined ticket but has a separate entrance, so follow signs from the main Alhambra pathway rather than backtracking.

periods.title: Granada Cathedral & Capilla Real
periods.text: Head into the city centre to visit Granada's Renaissance Cathedral (€5), one of Spain's largest, started in 1523 on the site of the main mosque. Next door, the Capilla Real (€5) holds the elaborate marble tombs of Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic monarchs who reconquered Granada in 1492. The sacristy museum displays Isabella's personal art collection including works by van der Weyden and Botticelli.
periods.tip: Buy a combined ticket for Cathedral and Capilla Real at either entrance. It saves €2 and avoids queuing twice.

periods.title: Flamenco at Sacromonte Cave
periods.text: Granada is the birthplace of a uniquely raw flamenco tradition rooted in the Sacromonte cave district. Book an evening zambra show (typically €25–35 including a drink) at one of the historic cave venues like Cueva de la Rocío or Cueva María la Canastera. The intimate cave settings, with low whitewashed ceilings, candlelight, and footstamping resonating off limestone, deliver an authenticity that stage theatres cannot replicate.
periods.tip: Book flamenco shows at least two days ahead. Minibuses run from Plaza Nueva up to Sacromonte, so check return times before you go.

periods.title: Arab Baths at Hammam Al Ándalus
periods.text: Start the final morning with a 90-minute session at Hammam Al Ándalus in the Albaicín (from €38), a beautifully restored Arab bathhouse modelled on Moorish hammams. Cold, warm, and hot pools, a steam room, and optional massage recreate a ritual that was central to Nasrid palace life. Booking the first session of the day means near-total silence and the baths largely to yourself.
periods.tip: Bring a swimsuit, as it is mandatory. Arrive 15 minutes early to change and rinse. Lockers are provided.

periods.title: Alcaicería Silk Market & Carmenes Gardens
periods.text: Explore the Alcaicería, the old Moorish silk market beside the Cathedral, now a narrow maze of spice stalls, ceramics, and leather goods. Haggle respectfully for hand-painted tiles or leather bags. Then seek out one of the hidden carmenes (private Moorish garden houses on the Albaicín hillside), some of which open for visits. The Carmen de los Mártires (free entry) has peacocks and rose gardens with Alhambra views.
periods.tip: The Carmen de los Mártires is often overlooked. It closes 14:00–17:00 on weekdays, so time your visit to arrive by 13:30.

periods.title: Final Tapas Trail Before Departure
periods.text: Granada's free tapas culture deserves a proper farewell. Walk the tapas trail from Calle Navas to Calle Elvira: order a beer or tinto de verano in four or five bars and you'll leave full without spending more than €15. Bar Los Diamantes is legendary for prawn tapas; Bodegas Castañeda for jamón and Manchego cheese. End with a coffee and a piece of piononos, Granada's signature cream pastry, at Café Ávila.
periods.tip: Tapas are free with each drink; you do not choose the tapa, as the bar decides. Embrace whatever arrives.

budgetTips.title: Book ahead online
budgetTips.text: Tickets and tours booked online are often 10-30% cheaper than walk-in prices. Many attractions sell out in peak season, so advance booking guarantees entry and saves money.

budgetTips.title: Visit in shoulder season
budgetTips.text: Shoulder months (just before or after peak season) offer better prices on accommodation and flights with similar weather and fewer crowds. Mar – Jun is peak.

budgetTips.title: Stay nearby, not at the gate
budgetTips.text: Accommodation directly at the attraction charges a premium. Staying 10-20 minutes away can save 30-50% on nightly rates. Use public transport or a rental car to bridge the gap.

budgetTips.title: Pack your own lunch
budgetTips.text: Tourist-area restaurants charge inflated prices. Pack sandwiches, snacks, and a refillable water bottle to save $15-30 per day on food. Buy supplies at local supermarkets or markets.

budgetTips.title: Free walking tours & guides
budgetTips.text: Many areas offer free or tip-based guided walks that are better than paid tours. Local guides provide insider knowledge and support the community. Check online for options.

budgetTips.title: Use local transport
budgetTips.text: Taxis and private transfers are the most expensive option. Local buses, shared minivans, or ride-sharing are 50-80% cheaper and give you a more authentic experience.

budgetBreakdown.notes: Street food → local restaurants → fine dining
Public buses → shared transfers → private car

practicalInfo.title: Entry & Visas
items: Keep a digital and physical copy of your passport, visa, and travel insurance at all times
Entry fees for Alhambra should be paid in EUR, so exchange money before arriving

practicalInfo.title: Health & Safety
items: Travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is essential
Bring a basic first aid kit with blister plasters, antiseptic, painkillers, and any personal medication
Sun protection is essential: apply SPF 50+ and reapply every 2 hours

practicalInfo.title: Getting Around
items: Excellent public transport, with trains, buses, and ferries connecting major points
Download offline maps before arriving, as mobile data coverage can be patchy in remote areas
Negotiate transport prices before departure or use metered taxis and ride-hailing apps

practicalInfo.title: Connectivity
items: Buy a local SIM card at the airport or any phone shop for affordable data, much cheaper than international roaming
WiFi is available at most accommodation but signal quality varies. Download offline maps and guides before heading to remote areas
Share your itinerary with someone at home and check in daily, especially for remote treks or island visits

practicalInfo.title: Money
items: Currency: EUR (Euro). Cards accepted in tourist areas, but carry cash for local vendors
ATMs are available in towns and cities. Visa and Mastercard are most widely accepted
Tip 5-10% or round up at restaurants. Guides and porters appreciate tips, so budget $5-10 per day per person

practicalInfo.title: Packing Tips
items: Comfortable walking shoes, layers for temperature changes, and a packable rain jacket
A reusable water bottle, headlamp, and portable phone charger are essential for any outdoor adventure
Quick-dry clothing is ideal, as you can wash and wear repeatedly, reducing pack weight

culturalTips.title: Respect Local Customs
culturalTips.text: Be mindful of local customs and traditions. Ask before photographing people. Learn basic greetings in the local language, as even a simple hello earns goodwill.

culturalTips.title: Leave No Trace
culturalTips.text: Pack out all rubbish. Stay on marked trails and paths. Do not touch, feed, or disturb wildlife. The natural beauty of Alhambra depends on every visitor treating it with respect. Take only photos, leave only footprints.

culturalTips.title: Photography Etiquette
culturalTips.text: Ask permission before photographing locals, especially in indigenous or traditional communities. Many religious sites have photography restrictions, so check signage and respect these rules. Drone regulations vary, so check local laws before flying.

culturalTips.title: Language & Communication
culturalTips.text: Learn a few words in Spanish, as greetings, please, thank you, and numbers go a long way. English is widely spoken in tourist areas but a translation app helps bridge gaps.

culturalTips.title: Support Local Communities
culturalTips.text: Choose locally-owned guesthouses, restaurants, and guides over international chains. Buy handicrafts directly from artisans. Your spending has the most impact when it goes directly into the local economy rather than through large tour operators.

culturalTips.title: Pace & Patience
culturalTips.text: Allow more time than you think, as rushing through natural and cultural sites misses the point. The best experiences come from slowing down and being present.
